core_obligations: Parts (1) and (2): combine the scheme-level geometric reducedness statements of this chapter with the algebra lemma on tensor products with a reduced algebra over a field, so that reducedness of Y (respectively geometric reducedness of X) is inherited by the product (proof lines 541-546).

Part (3): use the identification (X x_k Y) over kbar = X over kbar x over kbar Y over kbar together with part (2) and the definition of geometric reducedness, so that geometric reducedness of both factors passes to the product (proof lines 547-550).
Part (4): over a perfect field, reduced implies geometrically reduced, so part (3) applies and the product of reduced schemes over a perfect field is reduced (proof lines 550-551).
proof_roadmap: Reduce parts (1) and (2) to the algebra lemma on reduced base change, using the chapter's own point-wise statements (proof lines 541-546).
For part (3), pass to the algebraic closure where the product splits as a product over kbar and apply part (2) (proof lines 547-550).
For part (4), invoke the perfect-field statement to upgrade reducedness to geometric reducedness and apply part (3) (proof line 551).
difficulty_reason: The lemma collects four consequences of the interaction of reducedness with field base change: reducedness of the product at points over a geometrically reduced point, global reducedness of a product with a reduced factor, geometric reducedness of a product of geometrically reduced factors, and reducedness of a product over a perfect field (statement lines 526-536). Each part is short but they are assembled differently: (1) and (2) reduce to an algebra lemma on tensor products, (3) is obtained by passing to the algebraic closure and applying (2) there, and (4) upgrades reducedness to geometric reducedness over a perfect field before applying (3) (proof lines 541-551). What keeps this at H2 rather than lower is that the reductions are one-way and the reader has to see which of the two chapter lemmas feeds which part. The author also left the placeholder item (5) 'Add more here.' in the statement; it is reproduced verbatim as the author's own text.
